query: Refractory high-entropy alloys are promising structural materials, but achieving a strong combination of strength and plasticity remains important. What single intervention could improve this strength–plasticity combination? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate reference alloy, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a moderate amount of interstitial carbon (≈0.5 at%) to a refractory high-entropy alloy with a face‐centered cubic (FCC) matrix will enhance its strength–plasticity combination at room temperature by tuning the stacking fault energy to a level that promotes a synergy of deformation twinning (TWIP) and transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP).
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., one with a predominantly FCC matrix that exhibits TRIP behavior in its baseline state) produced without interstitials.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 0.5 atomic percent interstitial carbon during alloy synthesis/processing.
generation.conditions: Room temperature, under quasi-static tensile loading conditions; processing routes (e.g., casting and thermomechanical treatments) are kept identical aside from the carbon addition.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased stacking fault density and enhanced twin formation within the FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Interstitial carbon raises the stacking fault energy to an optimal level, stabilizing the FCC matrix while facilitating the onset of deformation twinning. This moderated energy environment allows both the TWIP and TRIP effects to operate synergistically, improving strain-hardening capability and postponing the onset of necking.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline alloy without carbon, the carbon-doped alloy is predicted to exhibit a simultaneous increase in tensile strength and ductility (e.g., improvements on the order of 10–20%, although the precise magnitude is uncertain), due to higher twin density and optimized phase stability.
generation.baseline: The identically processed refractory high-entropy alloy without carbon addition.
generation.boundary: This beneficial effect is expected only within a moderate carbon content; excessive carbon may lead to carbide precipitation, compromising ductility. Additionally, the improvement is anticipated in alloys with an FCC matrix predisposed to TRIP/TWIP behaviors at room temperature.
generation.uncertainty: The exact percentage improvements in mechanical properties depend on the alloy’s overall composition and processing conditions; detailed optimization may be required. It is also uncertain how sensitive the alloy is to slight deviations in carbon content.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the same refractory HEA: one set processed with an added 0.5 at% interstitial carbon and one baseline set without carbon. Both sets should be produced under identical conditions except for the carbon addition. Conduct room temperature tensile tests and carry out detailed microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM or EBSD) focusing on stacking fault and twin densities.
measurements: Density of stacking faults and twins in the microstructure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the baseline, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal increased stacking fault and twin formation, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: First, the addition of interstitial carbon into a recently developed TRIP-DP-HEA leads to an increase in stacking fault energy and hence phase stability. Tuning the stability of the face-centered cubic (f.c.c.) matrix phase in the dual-phase structure to a critical point triggers the twinning-induced plasticity (TWIP) effect while maintaining the TRIP effect, thereby further improving the alloy’s strain-hardening ability,. Second, HEAs benefit profoundly from interstitial solid solution strengthening instead of only the established massive solid solution strengthening provided by its multiple principle elements,. This is due to the circumstance that carbon, nitrogen and other interstitials lead to much higher lattice distortions than substitutional elements which strongly affects their interaction with dislocations,. We produced the interstitial HEA (iHEA) by melting and casting in a vacuum induction furnace using pure metals and carbon with nominal composition Fe49.5Mn30Co10Cr10C0.5 (at%).
